messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David is a 47-year-old bus driver who came to treatment months after a violent encounter with police that had begun to organize his life around vigilance, withdrawal, and mistrust. The incident happened late one evening after he had finished a route and was walking home from a corner store with a bag in his hand. A patrol car pulled up fast, officers got out shouting, and before he could make sense of what they wanted he was pushed against the hood, one hand forced behind his back while a flashlight was shone directly into his face. What stayed with him was not only the physical force but the sudden certainty that he could be harmed while trying to explain himself and no one nearby would intervene. He remembered seeing the badge, the cruiser lights reflecting in the store window, and the feeling that his face had ceased to belong to him, exposed and vulnerable under authority he could not challenge.

In the weeks afterward, the event returned to him abruptly. He could be driving his route and, without warning, the image of his cheek against the metal hood would flash into his mind so vividly that he lost track of the street for a moment. If a coworker asked what had happened that night, even being drawn into talking about it made his chest tighten and his thoughts scatter. The sight of police was especially potent. When a patrol car idled near a bus stop or an officer boarded downtown, he felt his body react before he had time to think. He would cover his face with his hands as if to block the view of himself, turn up loud music or the television as soon as he got home to drown out the memory, and increasingly avoid people who might ask questions or expect him to go out. The more he had come to believe that people could not be trusted and that the world was dangerous, the more sense it made to him to keep his distance and stay hidden; he also spoke with quiet bitterness about feeling cut off from the community he used to feel part of, as though the incident had severed something larger than his own sense of safety.

That same way of seeing the world kept the event close. Because he was certain danger could come from ordinary public places and from those meant to enforce order, police presence did not feel like a reminder of something over, but evidence that the threat was still current. Talking about the event felt risky for the same reason: in his mind, bringing it up meant exposing himself again. He watched people carefully and assumed bad intent quickly. On his bus he found himself scanning mirrors, stiffening when passengers argued, and struggling to concentrate on traffic whenever a cruiser appeared behind him. At home he checked the locks repeatedly, then checked them again, unable to settle with the thought that someone could come in. He had become more irritable as well, snapping at neighbors in the hallway and once shouting at a passenger who lingered near the front after asking an innocent question.

Those reactions pushed him further into the habits that were shrinking his life. When he felt wound up and unable to focus, he tried to manage it by avoiding others altogether after work, sitting alone in his apartment with the TV blaring, or literally hiding his face when he felt exposed. Repeated lock checking sometimes kept him up for an hour at night, and the exhaustion left him more short-tempered the next day. His efforts to shut things out did not bring relief for long. The loud noise in his apartment filled the silence but also made him feel more sealed off, and his self-imposed isolation deepened his conviction that he had lost his connection to other people and could not rely on anyone. Staying away from conversations about what happened gave him fewer chances to test whether someone might understand, so mistrust hardened rather than softened.

Over time the cycle tightened. Because he avoided people and buried himself in noise, the memory arrived unprocessed and abrupt, catching him off guard with the same force as before. Because he hid his face and withdrew whenever police were near, authority became more charged, not less; even a glimpse of a uniform through the bus windshield could set off a rush of anger, poor concentration, and the urge to get away. Those surges in turn confirmed for him that he was living in a dangerous world and had to stay on guard. The consequences had become concrete. He had started trading shifts to avoid downtown routes where police presence was heavier, and his supervisor had warned him about distractibility after he missed a stop announcement. What finally brought him in was a recent day when an officer stepped onto his bus and David froze, lost the thread of what a passenger was saying, and spent the rest of the route fighting the urge to cover his face. He said he was afraid that if this continued he would lose his job and whatever connection he still had to ordinary life, but he also held onto the hope that he might stop feeling as if danger was waiting in every uniform, every question, every knock at the door.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not clearly state in the same paragraph that David’s negative beliefs or appraisals cause triggers or reminders to occur or become more salient.
The vignette does not clearly state in the same paragraph that David’s sense of threat leads to or generates more negative appraisals or beliefs.
The vignette does not clearly state in the same paragraph that David’s sense of threat causes triggers or reminders to arise or become more potent.
The vignette does not clearly state in the same paragraph that David’s avoidance, safety behaviours, or other maladaptive strategies lead to triggers or reminders.
